claims.text: Introducing controlled coherent nanoprecipitates into tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys enhances high-temperature plastic strain and toughness.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission across phases.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces reduce stress localization at precipitate-matrix boundaries.
Relieving interfacial stress concentrations delays premature crack initiation.
Conventional processing of the proposed tungsten-based alloy produces random or incoherent precipitate distributions.
The SCCP process intentionally forms a high density of coherent nanoprecipitates.
Mechanical testing near 800 °C is relevant to fusion plasma-facing-component applications.
Dislocation-mediated plasticity is the dominant deformation mechanism in the proposed alloy regime up to approximately 800 °C.
SCCP-treated material will have higher high-temperature yield strength than an unmodified control.
SCCP-treated material will have greater plastic strain at high temperature than an unmodified control.
SCCP-treated material will have improved fracture toughness at high temperature.
Microstructural analysis will show widespread coherent interfaces assisting dislocation glide.
Refractory alloys exhibit a trade-off between high strength and tensile ductility.
The baseline alloy's low elevated-temperature ductility is caused by stress concentrations at incoherent interfaces.
The proposed mechanism should apply to tungsten-based and similar refractory high-entropy alloys up to approximately 800 °C.
The magnitude of property enhancement may vary with alloy composition, processing parameters, and test conditions.
The controlled comparison uses nominally identical tungsten-based alloys processed with SCCP or conventional processing and tests both at 800 °C.

Failure to obtain statistically significant mechanical-property improvements, or failure to observe coherent precipitates mediating dislocation transmission and stress relief, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
